passage:
February 14. Urmila, three months into managing the support team, opened a spreadsheet called "Year notes". Under Darshan she typed: "Stayed late to fix the billing outage. Calm with the angry client."
June 3. Another line: "Trained two new joiners; both say Darshan explains things best." Every few weeks she added lines for everyone on the team, good and bad.
December 9. Review week. Darshan's November had been rough: two missed tickets and a sharp email to a customer. Urmila's gut said "average at best". She opened the sheet and read eleven months of lines. Then she wrote the review: a strong year, a real dip in November, and a plan to fix it. Darshan read it and let out a long breath.

qa.q: What did Urmila note about Darshan in February?
qa.a: "Stayed late to fix the billing outage. Calm with the angry client."

qa.q: What was Urmila's gut telling her in December, and why didn't she simply follow it?
qa.a: It said 'average at best' because November's missed tickets were freshest, but she knew that feeling left out eleven months, so she checked her notes.

qa.q: What makes Urmila's review fair?
qa.a: It names the strong year and the real November dip together, with a plan to fix the dip, based on notes from every month.

qa.q: What does Darshan's long breath suggest?
qa.a: Relief, perhaps because Darshan expected to be judged on the bad November alone. 🙂

grounding: It shows a fair manager keeping notes all year so the review reflects every month, not just the latest.

passage: Hemant, before you write those reviews, let old Raghav tell you something. When I got my first team at the mill in Coimbatore, I was twenty-five and proud of my memory. In my first review round I gave our best dyer, Selvi, a poor rating because she'd spoiled one batch in March. March was the month before reviews. She had run the whole unit alone for six weeks in the monsoon, and I'd forgotten. She cried in the canteen. After that I kept a small diary, one page for each person, and wrote a line every Friday: good, bad, whatever happened. At review time I read the whole year first, before I trusted my gut. Selvi stayed with us nineteen years. Here, take this diary. It's blank. Start it this Friday.

qa.q: What mistake of Selvi's shaped that first review?
qa.a: She spoiled one batch in March.

qa.q: Why does Raghav still remember Selvi crying in the canteen?
qa.a: It showed Raghav how unfair a review based only on the latest month could feel to someone who had carried the unit alone.

qa.q: What habit is Raghav passing on to Hemant, and why?
qa.a: A diary with a page per person and a line every Friday, so reviews rest on the whole year instead of the last month.

qa.q: How might Hemant's team benefit from the blank diary?
qa.a: Their good months, not just their latest mistakes, will be on record when their reviews are written.

grounding: It shows a manager who learned to keep notes across the year so reviews cover every month, passing the habit on.

passage:
HR wanted the annual ratings by five, and at three o'clock Farhan's laptop refused to start, taking his notes file with it. For a moment he considered just going on memory. Memory said Naveen had been slow and distracted since Diwali.
Instead Farhan borrowed a colleague's laptop and opened his sent mail and the team calendar. Month by month he rebuilt the year: Naveen's January launch plan that the director praised, the April week he covered two roles, the July training he ran for the Nagpur office. Then the slower weeks since Diwali, which were real too.
At 4:52 he submitted: "Exceeds expectations for the year; recent slowdown discussed, support agreed." He messaged Naveen: "Can we talk tomorrow about how the last month has been for you?"

qa.q: What did Naveen run for the Nagpur office?
qa.a: The July training.

qa.q: Why did Farhan decide not to go on memory alone?
qa.a: He knew memory would mostly show the slow weeks since Diwali, and he wanted the rating to reflect the whole year.

qa.q: How did Farhan rebuild the year under time pressure?
qa.a: He used his sent mail and the team calendar to list each month's work, then rated the year while still naming the recent slowdown.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel reading Farhan's message?
qa.a: Naveen might feel cared for rather than judged, since Farhan asks how the last month has been instead of just marking him down.

grounding: It shows a fair manager, notes lost and time short, rebuilding the whole year so the rating isn't just the latest months.

passage:
On the third floor of the courier office in Kolkata, Pallavi, twenty-six, had one evening to write six annual reviews. She opened the small green notebook she had kept since January: one line per person, every month.
She started with Uday. Her memory said: December was a mess. He had misrouted forty parcels in the festival rush and snapped at a driver. She could still feel how angry she had been.
The notebook said more. March: "Built the new route sheet, cut delays." May: "Trained two new joiners, patient." August: "Covered night shifts for a week, no complaints." October: "Found the billing error." December: "Misrouted parcels in rush; tired, overworked?"
Pallavi put down her pen. Eleven good months and one hard one.
She wrote the December problem into the review, clearly, with a plan. Then she wrote the rest of the year too.

qa.q: How many parcels had Uday misrouted in December?
qa.a: He had misrouted forty parcels in the festival rush.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling about Uday before she opened the notebook?
qa.a: She still felt angry about December, and her memory was painting his whole year by that one bad month.

qa.q: Which habit made Pallavi's review fair?
qa.a: Keeping one line per person every month, so the review could show Uday's route sheet, training and night shifts alongside the December problem.

qa.q: What would change for Uday if Pallavi had written the review from memory alone?
qa.a: Uday would likely get a poor review based on one festival month, which would feel unfair after eleven months of good work and might make him give up trying.

grounding: It shows a fair manager using notes from the whole year so a review reflects all months, not only the latest memory.

"Just give Meenu a low rating, Jaya didi. You told me she messed up the launch last week."
"She did, Gautam. Pass me the phone."
"You're checking your phone for a review?"
"My notes. Every Friday I record one line about each person." Jaya scrolled. "Listen. February: Meenu stayed till midnight to fix the client file. April: she trained the new boy. June: best feedback from the Surat client."
"And last week?"
"Last week is here too. September: launch slides had errors, she owned it straight away."
Gautam put down his roti. "So what's the rating?"
"Good year, one bad week. That's what the notes say."
"I'd have remembered only the bad week."
"That's why I don't trust my memory, bhai."

qa.a: Every Friday she records one line about each person.

qa.q: Why doesn't Jaya trust her memory for the review?
qa.a: She knows the latest mistake would crowd out the good months, so she relies on her Friday notes instead of the freshest memory.

qa.q: Which choice by Jaya made her rating fair to Meenu?
qa.a: Checking her notes for the whole year, so the launch errors sit next to the late nights, the training and the client praise.

qa.q: How does Gautam's view of Meenu change during the conversation?
qa.a: Gautam starts ready to rate Meenu low for one week, but after hearing the notes he admits he would have remembered only the bad week.

grounding: It shows a fair manager keeping notes across the whole year so a performance review reflects every month, not just the most recent memory.

passage: My first year as a team lead, I nearly got Aparna's review badly wrong. I'm Gurpreet, and I manage four people at a design studio in Mohali. In November, Aparna missed two deadlines, and that was all I could think about when I sat down to write her review. Then I opened the file I'd been keeping, one line per person per month, a habit borrowed from my old boss. January: led the school-app redesign. April: trained the new intern. July: stayed late to fix a client's crash. November: two missed deadlines, also her father's surgery. Reading it all together, the year looked completely different. I rated her 'exceeds expectations', and we talked about November separately, gently. She cried a little and said nobody had ever remembered April.

qa.q: What did Aparna do in April?
qa.a: Aparna trained the new intern.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel before opening the file, and what changed?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt frustrated and fixed on November's missed deadlines; reading the whole year's notes brought a calmer, fairer view.

qa.q: What habit made Gurpreet's review fair, and why?
qa.a: Keeping one line per person per month, so the review reflects every month and not just the freshest memory.

qa.q: Why might Aparna have cried when April was mentioned?
qa.a: Aparna probably felt seen and relieved that work from months ago was remembered, especially after a hard November.

grounding: Shows a manager using notes kept across the whole year so a review reflects all months, not just the latest.

passage:
HR head's note, hotel front office, year-end reviews, 12 December.
I sat in on Pema's reviews today; it's her first year managing the front desk. Tushar was up first. Everyone knows he mishandled a big group check-in last week, and I expected Pema to open with it. She didn't. She opened a small notebook with a page for each month. "February, you calmed down the family whose booking we lost. June, you trained two new staff on the system. September, three guest letters named you." Only then did she raise last week, calmly, as one item. Tushar's shoulders came down from his ears. Afterwards I asked where the notebook habit came from. "My first boss judged me on one bad week," she said. I've asked her to show the other managers her method in January.

qa.q: How many guest letters named Tushar in September?
qa.a: Three guest letters named him in September.

qa.q: Why did Pema choose to open with February rather than last week?
qa.a: Pema, remembering how unfair it felt to be judged on one bad week, felt determined to give Tushar's whole year its proper weight.

qa.q: What could other managers learn from Pema's notebook?
qa.a: Keeping a page per month means reviews cover the whole year, and a recent mistake can be raised calmly as one item among many.

qa.q: How did the review feel for Tushar?
qa.a: Tushar arrived tense, expecting to be judged on last week's check-in, and relaxed as his whole year was recognised.

grounding: Shows a young manager using monthly notes so a review reflects the whole year, not just last week's mistake.

passage:
30 March, late
Reviews tomorrow. Jatin's is the hard one. All I can see is last month: the parents' complaint about Class 6 marks, the lab left unlocked. My gut says 'needs improvement'.
But I promised myself this year I wouldn't do reviews from memory. So I opened my review file, the one I add to every Friday. Jatin, June: started the science club, twenty kids signed up. August: covered for Seema ma'am for three weeks without a word of complaint. November: his class had the best practical scores in the school. February: the complaint and the lab.
So: one rough month out of ten. I'll still talk to him about the lab, clearly. But 'needs improvement' was my tired brain talking. Changing it to 'good, with one area to work on'.
Nandini

qa.q: What did Jatin start in June?
qa.a: Jatin started the science club, and twenty kids signed up.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling before opening the review file?
qa.a: Nandini felt tense and doubtful about Jatin, because last month's complaint and the unlocked lab filled Nandini's mind.

qa.q: Why is adding to the review file every Friday a good habit?
qa.a: It captures each month as it happens, so the review can weigh all ten months instead of the freshest memory.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel if he had been rated 'needs improvement'?
qa.a: Jatin might feel hurt and unseen, since the science club, the three weeks of cover and the practical scores would have been ignored.

grounding: Shows a young coordinator using notes kept all year so a teacher's review reflects every month, not just the last.

passage: At the women's dairy cooperative in Anand district, Aditi had been the young manager for a year. Review time came in March, and her first thought about Sarita, the collection supervisor, was the mess in February: two days of spoiled milk when a chiller broke. That was all she could remember. But Aditi had a habit. Every month she wrote a few lines in a green register about each supervisor. She sat under the neem tree and read Sarita's page. April: trained six new collectors. June: stayed till midnight during the monsoon flooding. September: found the fault in the testing machine. December: collection up by a tenth. February: chiller problem, not her fault, but slow to report it. Aditi wrote the review: "An excellent year. One lesson: report equipment faults at once." Sarita read it twice and smiled.

qa.q: How many new collectors did Sarita train in April?
qa.a: Six new collectors.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she first thought about Sarita's review?

qa.q: Which habit helped Aditi write a fair review?
qa.a: Writing a few lines each month in the green register, so the review covered the whole year instead of the latest memory.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt reading the review?
qa.a: Sarita seemed pleased and fairly treated, seeing a whole year of work counted, with one clear lesson.

grounding: Shows a fair manager using monthly notes so a performance review reflects the whole year, not just the most recent problem.

passage: In the Madrid office, performance reviews were due on Friday. Ines, a new team manager, sat down to write Layla's. Her mind went straight to November: Layla had missed a deadline, and a client had complained. It felt like the whole story. But in January Ines had started a small habit: a note on her phone after each week, a line per person. She opened it. February: Layla stayed late to finish the pitch. April: suggested the new filing system everyone now uses. July: covered for two colleagues on leave. September: best client feedback in the team. November: missed deadline; she had been sick that week, Ines now remembered. Ines deleted her first draft. The new one began: "A strong year with one difficult month." When they met, Layla looked relieved. "I thought November was all you'd remember." "It almost was," Ines admitted.

qa.q: When did Layla suggest the new filing system?
qa.a: In April.

qa.q: What was Ines feeling when she first thought of Layla's review?
qa.a: Ines felt sure and a bit annoyed, with November's missed deadline seeming like the whole story.

qa.q: What habit helped Ines, and why is it worth copying?
qa.a: A weekly note on her phone for each person, which gives a record of the whole year so recent events don't dominate.

grounding: Shows a fair manager using weekly notes so a performance review reflects the whole year, not just the latest memory.

passage:
In the small meeting room of the city library, Charu opened the folder she had kept since January before Joseph's yearly review.
Joseph came in tense. The last month had been rough: he had mixed up two event dates, and a school group had turned up to a locked hall. He expected that to be the whole review.
"Let's go month by month," Charu said. She had a page for each. February: he set up the children's reading corner. April: he cleared the late-return backlog. July: three thank-you letters from readers. September: he helped train the new assistant. November: the date mix-up.
"I'd forgotten half of this," Joseph said.
"So had I, until I read my notes this morning," Charu admitted. "That's why I keep them."
They spent five minutes on November: what went wrong and what would help. The rest of the hour was about the other months.

qa.q: What happened in November?
qa.a: Joseph mixed up two event dates, and a school group turned up to a locked hall.

qa.q: Why does Charu admit she had forgotten half of it too?
qa.a: Charu feels honest and a little humble, knowing her own memory favours the latest month, which is why she trusts the notes.

qa.q: How does Charu's folder make the review fairer?
qa.a: A page for each month means the whole year counts, so one bad November doesn't outweigh the reading corner or July's letters.

qa.q: What is the review like for Joseph?
qa.a: Joseph goes from tense to relieved, seeing his whole year counted and not just the mix-up.

grounding: Shows a fair manager who keeps month-by-month notes so a yearly review reflects the whole period, not the latest memory.

passage:
Dear Kavitha,
Before we meet on Friday for your annual review, I want to explain how I prepared, because I know the last few weeks have been hard for you.
If I went only by memory, I'd mostly remember October: the missed supplier call and the rushed report. That's what my mind throws up first. So I didn't go by memory. Since January I've kept a short note every Friday for everyone on the team.
Reading yours, I found the new filing system you built in February, the angry customer you calmed in May, the two weeks you covered for a colleague on leave in July, and the training session you ran in August. October is in there too, and we'll talk about it honestly.
But it's one month out of ten. Your review will be about all ten.
See you on Friday.
Gurpreet

qa.q: Since when has Gurpreet kept Friday notes?
qa.a: Gurpreet has kept a short note every Friday since January.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet not trust memory for the review?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt wary that memory would throw up October first, and wanted to be fair to all of Kavitha's year.

qa.q: What does the Friday note habit do for the review?
qa.a: It brings back February's filing system, May's customer, July's cover and August's training, so one hard month doesn't define the review.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel reading the letter before Friday?
qa.a: Kavitha would likely feel relieved and less anxious, knowing October will be discussed but the whole year counts.

grounding: Shows a fair manager who keeps notes all year so a review covers every month, not just the most recent one.

passage:
Jeevan, you're a new manager now, so here's what I wish someone had told me. I'm Rukmini, and my first round of reviews was a disaster.
I had six people. I sat down the night before and wrote whatever came to mind. For one designer, all I could think of was the logo she'd got wrong the week before. I wrote "needs improvement". She cried in the meeting and then showed me her work from the year: the festival campaign, the new website, two awards. All forgotten, by me, her own manager.
I felt sick. I apologised and redid the review.
Since then I keep a notes file for each person. Every other Friday, ten minutes, three lines: something good, something to work on, anything I noticed. At review time I read the whole year before I write a word.
It sounds boring. It's the fairest thing I do.

qa.q: How many people did Rukmini review in the first round?
qa.a: Rukmini had six people to review.

qa.q: What did Rukmini feel when the designer showed the year's work?
qa.a: Rukmini felt sick and ashamed, realising a whole year of good work had been forgotten because of one recent mistake.

qa.q: What is Rukmini's notes routine, and why does it help?
qa.a: Every other Friday, ten minutes, three lines for each person, so the whole year is on paper before any review is written.

qa.q: What was that first review like for the designer?
qa.a: The designer felt hurt and unseen, rated 'needs improvement' over one logo despite a year of strong work.

grounding: Shows a manager who learned to keep notes across the year so reviews reflect all months, not only the latest memory.

passage:
Review week in our office always smells of burnt coffee. This year I sat beside Chinmay, our manager, while he prepared for Rukmini's appraisal, and I noticed something odd. He didn't open last month's reports first. He opened a thin notebook with a tab for every month, January to December.
"March: stayed late to rescue the vendor file," he read, half to himself. "July: quiet, but trained two interns."
Rukmini had a rough November; people still talked about the client complaint at lunch. I expected it to sink her review. Instead Chinmay wrote one line about November and four about the rest of the year.
When she came out, she caught my eye and mouthed, "He remembered March, Yash."
I can't say what went on in his head. But I've started keeping my own notebook.

qa.q: What did Chinmay's notebook have a tab for?
qa.a: It had a tab for every month, January to December.

qa.q: What might Yash have felt when Rukmini mouthed that Chinmay remembered March?
qa.a: Yash was probably surprised and reassured, having expected the November complaint to sink her review, and then seeing the whole year counted.

qa.q: What could other managers learn from Chinmay's approach?
qa.a: They could jot a short note every month, so a review weighs the whole year rather than the latest mistake.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see her review if only November had counted?
qa.a: She would likely feel judged by one bad month, with her March rescue and the rest of her year ignored.

grounding: Shows a manager who keeps notes across every month so a performance review reflects the whole year, not only recent memory.
